To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) most optimization techniques for registration areas can be represented using metrical task system models; (b) some of these representations are simple while others can be intricate; (c) the simple representations imply that general lower bounds carry over to our location management formulations; (d) some restricted models have better algorithms.

(a) the optimization techniques used in the literature for location management can be modeled as metrical task systems and (b) some restricted models are much simpler and have better performance guarantees.

(i) the optimization techniques used for registration area based management can be modeled as metrical task systems, (ii) these models directly imply the applica- bility of known results on on-line algorithms for metrical task systems for location management, and (iii) some restricted models in location management admit much better (and simple) algorithms than the ones implied by the general results on on-line metrical task systems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and analysis of algorithms for the registration area location management problem, which is one of the most fundamental issues in mobile computing.
the following questions: What is the best we can hope for in terms of the performance of on-line location management algorithms?
the design of optimal online algorithms for location management.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the problem of designing good algorithms for location management is very hard.

there is little to gain from optimization techniques such as overlapped registration areas and forwarding pointers, and the only advantage is that they are simpler to implement than optimal algorithms.
the problem of designing optimal online algorithms is intractable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best known algorithms for these models are within a factor of 2 of the lower bounds.
most optimization techniques proposed in the literature are sub-optimal in the worst case.
the best possible performance for location management is still not known.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a careful study of optimization techniques for location management can lead to a better understanding of the tradeoffs involved and the applicability of these techniques.
the design of algorithms for location management in cellular networks can be viewed as the problem of designing optimal on-line algorithms for metrical task systems.

the design and analysis of online algorithms for location management can be carried out in the context of online algorithms for metrical task systems and that this approach provides a unified view of existing techniques.
